does: Rubs a halved ripe tomato, cut side down, over the large holes of a box grater until only the flat skin is left in the hand. The pulp falls through as a loose, fresh sauce with no skin to pick out, ready to cook down or to spread on bread.

intro.what: A ripe tomato is rubbed cut side down on a grater, so the pulp falls through and the skin stays behind.
intro.why: It gives a smooth fresh tomato pulp in moments without peeling or a blender.

how: Cut the ripe tomatoes in half across their middle.
Hold a half by its skin and rub the cut side over the large holes of a grater set in a bowl.
Stop when only the flat skin is left in your hand, and throw the skin away.

cues.text: A loose red pulp collects in the bowl and a thin flat skin is left in the hand.
The flesh gives easily against the grater. A hard tomato resists.

mistakes.mistake: Using hard, pale tomatoes, which give little pulp and a sour taste.
mistakes.fix: Use ripe, soft, deep red tomatoes.

mistakes.mistake: Grating on the fine holes, which tears the skin into the pulp.
mistakes.fix: Use the large holes and keep the skin flat against your palm.

quiz.question: Which side of the tomato meets the grater?
quiz.because: The flesh grates through and the skin stays behind as a sheet.

quiz.question: Which tomatoes grate best?
quiz.because: Ripe tomatoes give plenty of sweet pulp.

variant_of.differs: Only the soft flesh is grated, from a cut half held by its skin, and the skin is left behind and thrown away. The result is a pulp, not shreds.
